Measurement. In quantum mechanics, measurement refers to the act of observing or extracting information from a quantum system, which fundamentally alters its state. A quantum system exists in a superposition of states until measured. Upon measurement, the wavefunction collapses to a single eigenstate corresponding to the observed result. This counterintuitive phenomenon—that observation itself influences reality—lies at the heart of quantum weirdness and remains philosophically contentious.

A quantum system before measurement is described by a wavefunction that is a superposition of multiple possible states, each with an associated probability amplitude. Upon measurement of an observable like position or energy, the wavefunction collapses irreversibly. The outcome is one eigenvalue of the corresponding operator, with probability given by the squared amplitude.

The uncertainty principle limits what can be simultaneously known. Measuring position precisely destroys knowledge of momentum and vice versa. The product of the uncertainty in position and the uncertainty in momentum is greater than or equal to h-bar divided by two. Wave-particle duality is intimately tied to measurement. Particles exhibit wave-like interference until measured, at which point they choose a single particle-like path.

In quantum entanglement, measuring one particle instantaneously tells an entangled partner what to be, collapsing its superposition at spacelike separation. Einstein called this spooky action at a distance. The measurement problem is unsolved philosophically. Interpretations like Copenhagen, which holds that the wavefunction is real but collapses upon measurement; many-worlds, which holds that collapse is illusory and measurement branches the universe; and pilot-wave, which is deterministic, each propose different mechanisms.

Repeated measurements of the same system in the same state yield identical results, showing predictability. Different states yield distributions matching quantum predictions—evidence that measurement's physical action is real.

Superposition is the quantum state that measurement collapses. Wavefunction collapse is the mechanism by which measurement changes the system. Wave-particle duality is the dual nature revealed by measurement context. In quantum entanglement, measurement of one particle affects an entangled partner instantaneously. The uncertainty principle is a fundamental limit on simultaneous measurement precision. Quantum mechanics is the framework in which measurement's strange behavior occurs.
